q: Which specific genetic loci or DDR pathway variants drive the ~2x spread in HZE relaxation time tau across the 15 inbred strains, and does the (tau_HZE, q_HZE) phenotype map to known Trp53/Atm/Brca1/53bp1/H2ax variant classes?
basis: Fig. 6 identifies MegaMUGA SNP peaks but the genotype file is not deposited (DATA-BLOCKED at replication level), and Table 1A per-particle Pearson matrix is unreproducible. The paper leaves the mechanistic gap: strain-level tau is observed, but the causal genetic driver is only speculated from SNP peaks near candidate DDR genes. Without per-strain, per-particle (tau, q, RIFmax) plus the SNP calls, we cannot rank candidate loci by effect size on repair kinetics.
next_steps: (1) Request MegaMUGA genotypes + per-cell foci counts from Costes lab under a data-use agreement; (2) intersect strain-level tau_HZE rank order with published Trp53/Atm/H2ax variant panels for the same 15 inbred strains (Mouse Phenome Database); (3) run eQTL-style regression of tau on cis-SNPs within a 500kb window of the 8 core DDR genes; (4) validate hits by CRISPR knock-in of the candidate variant into a reference strain and re-measuring 53BP1 kinetics.

q: Does the ex-vivo skin fibroblast 53BP1 repair phenotype actually predict in-vivo tissue-specific tumorigenesis, or is the Fig. 7B / 7C signal an artifact of small-n over-fitting across 10 CC strains and 4 MTB strains?
basis: Fig. 7B r=0.61, n=10 yields derived p_two-sided ~0.061 (borderline non-significant), and Fig. 7C at n=4 has an analytical critical |r|=0.950 with zero organs surviving Bonferroni across 19 organs. The paper's central translational claim ('ex-vivo predicts in-vivo susceptibility') is therefore statistically thin. Whether this reflects a true small underlying effect or an over-fit to noise is unresolved.
next_steps: (1) Enlarge the CC cohort to ~30 strains (feasible via UNC Collaborative Cross resource) to bring Fig. 7B to n>=20 where r=0.6 becomes robustly significant; (2) reduce the organ multiple-comparison burden by pre-registering 3-4 organs of highest biological interest before the analysis; (3) run a leave-one-strain-out cross-validation of the predictive claim; (4) attempt an orthogonal readout (gammaH2AX foci or comet assay) on the same strains to test whether ANY DSB kinetic marker predicts in-vivo cancer, not just 53BP1.

q: How stable is the (tau, q, RIFmax) fit under alternative time-sampling and noise-model assumptions --- specifically, do 4 time points at 0.5/2/4/24 h post-irradiation actually identify all three parameters, or does the paper's fit collapse to an effective 2-parameter surface with RIFmax and q trading off?
basis: The original-pass identifiability MC (CLAIM 11) passed under the paper's stated noise model, but the paper never reports the parameter covariance matrix or profile-likelihoods. With only 4 non-uniform time points and biexponential decay + residual plateau, RIFmax and q are known to be near-degenerate for tau in the 2-8 h range (much of the observed strain spread). If this degeneracy is real, the reported strain-level (tau, q) may be aliased.
next_steps: (1) Recompute the Fisher information matrix at each strain's best-fit (tau, q, RIFmax) and report condition number; (2) run a bootstrap over synthetic 4-point samples with the paper's stated Poisson foci-count noise, report joint 95% credible regions for (tau, q); (3) simulate a 6-time-point protocol (adding 8 h and 48 h) and quantify how much the parameter uncertainty shrinks; (4) publish this as a design-of-experiment recommendation for follow-up ex-vivo studies.

q: Does the strain-level ordering of DDR kinetics translate to human inter-individual variability, and can a 53BP1 foci assay on human primary fibroblasts (LCLs or dermal punch biopsies) recover a comparable dynamic range predictive of radiotherapy toxicity?
basis: The paper's motivation is human-radiotherapy prediction, but it never bridges from mouse strains to human individuals. The ~2x tau range across inbred mice is a floor estimate for the range in outbred humans, and it is unknown whether the assay format transfers cleanly (dose calibration, foci-detection thresholds, background 53BP1 foci from replication stress differ between species).
next_steps: (1) Adopt the ex-vivo protocol on a panel of 30-50 human LCLs from the 1000 Genomes reference set spanning ancestry groups; (2) benchmark against archived clinical radiotherapy toxicity cohorts (REQUITE, RAPPER); (3) cross-check with existing radiogenomic GWAS hits for late toxicity (SNPs near TGFB1, XRCC1, ATM); (4) publish a species-bridging equivalence table before proposing the assay as a clinical stratifier.

q: Given the near-complete lack of data deposition (no supplement, no figshare/Zenodo/GitHub, no raw foci counts, no genotypes), what curation or re-analysis of the underlying NASA Space Radiation Laboratory (NSRL) beamline campaigns would be needed to make Pariset 2020 fully reproducible in the FAIR sense?
basis: Re-pass full-text parse confirmed NO deposited data. This is downstream of a multi-year NSRL campaign involving 76 mice x 15 strains x 3 LETs x multiple doses --- an expensive, non-reproducible-from-scratch dataset. Yet no per-cell foci table, no per-mouse metadata, no beamline dosimetry log is published. This is the largest single reproducibility gap and blocks Table 1A entirely.
next_steps: (1) Contact NSRL / NASA HRP data-archive coordinators to determine whether the raw foci counts and per-mouse dosimetry ARE archived internally but not linked; (2) if so, propose a re-release to a FAIR repository (Zenodo with restricted-access data-use agreement); (3) if not, propose a limited re-collection focused on the 4 Table 2 strains that failed our quadrant match, to disambiguate paper-vs-digitization noise; (4) draft a companion 'data supplement' paper with per-strain, per-particle (tau, q, RIFmax) tables that the community can rebuild Table 1A from.
